source: Pleiss, Schiffer, von Weizsaecker (2026) Disentangling generalization and memorization in LLMs using chess
finding: Reopened and read in full (checker gap 5). More reasoning effort cuts error in every tier, but the gain per 1,000 reasoning tokens is smaller where priors are scarce. The model also spends many more tokens on unfamiliar positions.
numbers: GPT-5, minimal vs moderate reasoning effort. Total ACPL fell 71.74%: 85.3% in ND, 77.25% in WD, 64.69% in OOD. Moderate-effort ACPL: 11.72 (WD) vs 298.81 (OOD). OOD/WD ACPL ratio widens from about 16x (minimal) to about 25x (moderate). Mean reasoning tokens: 3,426 (WD), 11,800 (ND), 16,953 (OOD). Relative gain per 1,000 tokens: 22.55% (WD), 7.23% (ND, -67.98%), 3.81% (OOD, -83.10%).
quote: relative performance gains per token diminish as the density of relevant priors decreases
limits: One model (GPT-5) for the reasoning contrast, one prompt (FEN in, move out), no retrieval arm. Total relative ACPL drop is not monotone (ND 85.3% beats WD 77.25%). The per-1,000-token metric is partly an artefact of OOD using 5x more tokens. Familiarity is inferred from opening and engine statistics, not from known training data.
agent_relevance: Supports the idea that thinking tokens are worth less on unfamiliar problems, but the effect is a rate effect, not a ceiling: OOD still improves 64.69%. No test of whether retrieved patterns restore the rate. That test is still missing.

source: Pleiss et al. (2026), limits and rule-following section
finding: The authors say plainly that the link between prior density and error is an association, not a proven cause. Illegal moves are the sturdier finding: legality is a bounded check, yet extra reasoning does not remove the failures.
numbers: GPT-5 with moderate reasoning still proposes illegal moves in more than 10% of OOD positions while using about 5x the reasoning tokens of WD positions. Legality failures persist across output notations (appendix G.3) and under a roughly fivefold rise in reasoning tokens. Human control: speed pressure slowed humans but did not reduce rule accuracy.
quote: we do not claim to identify a causal effect of prior density net of all co-varying positional properties
limits: No dedicated human study on the same positions (authors say it would be needed). Co-varying positional properties are not ruled out.
agent_relevance: Treat the first candidate from a weak pattern match as unverified. A cheap legality or constraint check should stay on even when thinking is long. This fits guardrail-style checks in the schema.

source: Sala & Gobet (2017) Experts' memory superiority for domain-specific random material generalizes across fields of expertise: a meta-analysis
finding: Full text read (checker gap 8). Experts recall random material better than novices across domains. The raw effect is moderate and shrinks after a bias correction, but stays significant.
numbers: Random-effects model, k = 28 effect sizes (24 studies, N = 903): r = .41, 95% CI [.29, .51], I2 = 63.06%. Funnel plot asymmetric. Trim-and-fill trimmed 8 studies: r = .29, 95% CI [.17, .41]. Fail-safe N = 745. Binomial check: experts beat novices in 49 of 55 experiments (p = 9.11e-10). Sensitivity analysis dropping two weak studies: r = .28, CI [.15, .40], 7 studies filled in.
quote: significant, but at best moderate, a result consistent with the chunking hypothesis
limits: Small number of studies and participants, so no moderator tests on age, gender or expertise level. Randomisation methods differ by domain. Several excluded studies lacked data to compute an effect size (the authors say most of them also showed a skill effect).
agent_relevance: So the 'small but real' random-board edge is not just publication bias: about r = .29 survives correction. It is no more than moderate, which matches a chunk-based account (stored patterns help a little even without structure). For our agent: expect a small residual gain from memory on structure-shuffled tasks, not zero and not large.

source: Sala & Gobet (2017) meta-analysis, moderator tables
finding: Domain was a marginal moderator; time of exposure was not. Music is the outlier. Games (mostly chess) sit at r = .42, in line with the pooled value.
numbers: Domain moderator Q(4) = 8.69, p = .069 (k = 28): games r = .42 [.25,.56] k = 11; music r = .69 [.35,.86] k = 5; programming r = .36 [.21,.49] k = 6; sports r = .30 [-.04,.58] k = 3 (ns); other r = .24 [-.09,.52] k = 3 (ns). Exposure time (> 8 s vs <= 8 s): Q(1) = 0.89, p = .346, k = 24. After sensitivity cut, domain p = .116 and time p = .420.
limits: Chess has the only continuous expertise variable (Elo), so only chess studies could be coded by Elo. Sports and 'other' intervals include zero. The null on exposure time contrasts with Gobet & Simon 2000 (master slope slightly larger with time in random positions). The authors note effect size is inversely related to how random the material is.
agent_relevance: The slot-and-core story predicts that exposure time should help experts more. The pooled data do not show it, so do not build a scaffold rule that assumes longer retrieval time helps experts specifically.

source: Li et al. (2026) SkillsBench: Benchmarking How Well Agent Skills Work Across Diverse Tasks (v4)
finding: Gap 4. Curated skills help on average. Skills the agent writes for itself do worse than no skills at all, on all three tested harness-model pairs. The trajectory audit gives four reasons.
numbers: 87 tasks, 8 domains, 18 model-harness configurations: no skills 33.9% to curated 50.5% (+16.6 pp; range +4.1 to +25.7). Self-generated (3 configs): Claude Code + Opus 4.7 43.0 -> 34.9 (-8.1 pp; curated +18.2); Codex + GPT-5.5 46.8 -> 35.5 (-11.3; curated +19.7); Gemini CLI + Gemini 3.1 Pro 36.0 -> 24.5 (-11.5; curated +24.8). Audit of 12 trajectories: in 10 of 12 Codex/Gemini ones the generated skills were never read.
quote: Self-generated Skills land below the no-Skills baseline on all three configurations
limits: Table rows are garbled in the PDF text; the -8.1/-11.3/-11.5 deltas and the matched curated gains are quoted from the text. This is a later version than the SoK's -1.3 figure (v1-era), so the -1.3 and the -8 to -11 numbers are not the same measurement. Self-generation here includes creator/solver interference, so part of the loss is workflow, not content.
agent_relevance: The harm of self-written skills is real and larger in the newer version. Unread skills and confident wrong content are failure modes our admission rule must catch: check that a template is retrieved and used, and test it on cases it was not written from.

source: Li et al. (2026) SkillsBench, quantity and complexity ablations
finding: Gap 6 (human-style cap). Fewer, compact skills beat many or long ones. Gain does not rise with number of items past 2-3.
numbers: Gain by skills per task: 1 skill +18.0 pp; 2-3 skills +19.0 pp; 4 or more +10.1 pp. Gain by length: compact +19.0, standard +21.5, detailed +14.5, comprehensive +0.7 pp. Abstract: focused skills with at most three modules beat bigger bundles. Skills hurt on 13 of 87 tasks (largest -7.4 pp), caused by a single heavy pipeline with no fallback.
limits: Observational split of tasks by how many skills were bundled, not a randomised arm, and tokens are not held equal (more skills = more tokens). Curated skills, not templates with slots.
agent_relevance: Consistent with a 'few rich items' cap, but also with 'less context overhead'. For the schema: cap retrieved items at about 3, keep each compact, and give each a fallback and an applicability boundary.

source: Xu & Wu (2026) Skill Availability and Presentation Granularity in LLM Agents: A Controlled SkillsBench Study
finding: Gap 1 (nearest controlled test). Having a skill matters; how it is written (principles vs checklist, with or without one worked example) matters little and varies by model.
numbers: 30-task subset, two models (GPT-5.5, DeepSeek V4-Flash), six skill conditions, 5 trials per cell, 1,800 rows. Skill vs no skill: +26.7 to +36.0 pp (GPT-5.5) and +18.0 to +26.0 pp (DeepSeek). Low vs high abstraction: +0.7 pp (GPT-5.5), -6.7 pp (DeepSeek), both CIs cross zero. Adding one worked example: +0.7 and +1.3 pp.
limits: Not a slot-filled template test and not equal-token (a worked example adds tokens). 30 tasks; wide intervals. Abstraction here means writing style, not variable slots.
agent_relevance: No evidence that a fixed core plus variables beats a plain description. Slot-filling is not shown to be worth its cost, and the right call is to test it before building it.

source: How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents: An Empirical Study of Experience-Following Behavior (2025)
finding: Gap 4. Adding every finished run to memory hurts. Adding only runs that pass a strict check helps, and a weak automatic check is not enough.
numbers: Four agents, add-all vs fixed memory vs coarse automatic judges (C1-C3) vs strict (ground-truth) check. RegAgent success: fixed 67.53, add-all 55.48, C1 63.18, C3 67.35, strict 70.95. EHRAgent acc: fixed 16.75, add-all 13.05, strict 38.50. AgentDriver: fixed 40.11, add-all 32.32, strict 51.00. CIC-IoT: fixed 71.50, add-all 59.90, strict 85.40. A judge fine-tuned on only 300 trajectories (C3) already beat unfiltered adding.
limits: Strict check uses ground-truth correctness, which our agent often will not have. One synthetic agent (RegAgent) is built to follow experience strongly. Memory sizes differ across arms.
agent_relevance: Admission needs a trustworthy outcome signal. A held-out or verifier-based success signal works; the model grading itself does not. Unfiltered add-all fell 4 to 12 points below the fixed starting memory in all four agents.

source: How Memory Management Impacts LLM Agents (2025), experience-following and deletion
finding: Gap 4. Agents copy the most similar stored run (experience following), so one bad record spreads. Removing records by their later reuse success (retrieved at least n times, mean utility below a threshold) helps when the utility judge is reliable.
numbers: Output similarity tracks input similarity (near-perfect correlation, Pearson r about 1, with add-all/coarse memory). History-based deletion rule: delete if retrieved at least 5 times and mean utility below 0.3 (coarse) or 0.7 (strict); combined periodic + history deletion cut memory size most. With a strict judge, history-based deletion improved a non-synthetic agent. With a GPT-4o-mini judge it helped EHRAgent but hurt AgentDriver.
limits: Utility judge quality decides everything. Distribution-shift test: periodic deletion helped stabilise on EHRAgent. Exact table gains for deletion not extracted (table text garbled).
agent_relevance: This is the best direct support for a 'reuse count plus reuse success' admission and retirement rule. Count how often a template is retrieved and whether the run it cued succeeded, then retire low scorers.

source: Nguyen, Nguyen, Vuong (2026) Recursive Self-Evolving Agents via Held-Out Selection (RSEA)
finding: Gap 4. A strict held-out keep-better gate stops evolved context from hurting. Without a gate, the same method overfits, and an online method with no gate (Dynamic Cheatsheet) collapses on one benchmark.
numbers: Six baselines, four benchmarks, one backbone. ALFWorld (134 tasks x 5 seeds, 7B) success: ReAct 64.6, AWM 65.4, ACE 66.9, DC 70.7, RSEA 69.3 (p = 0.015 vs ReAct). WebShop score: ReAct 0.429, DC 0.136 (collapse), RSEA 0.437. tau-bench retail: ReAct 41.7, AWM 51.7, DC 36.7. No-gate ablation: 100% in-sample but 66.7% test (33-point gap) vs 67.3% with gate; ReAct 63.6%. Layer ablation: skills-only and playbook-only 69.8%; full state 68.5% (layers overlap).
limits: Small test sets (GAIA 30 tasks, tau-bench 60). Single shared local backbone (7B on ALFWorld, 30B elsewhere). Gains on ALFWorld are a few points and the dev pool was only 30 tasks.
agent_relevance: A strict keep-better gate on a disjoint split is a cheap admission rule that bounded downside to roughly zero in this study. It also shows no artefact wins everywhere: the wrong store can cost 29 points (DC on WebShop).

source: Pham et al. (2026) Reliable Memory from Unstable Growth: Curating Self-Written Agent Playbooks with Randomized Experiments (RBC)
finding: Gap 4. The same memory-writing procedure can write a helpful or a harmful playbook, and the agent's own helpful/harmful tags do not tell which. Measuring each block of lessons by random inclusion on practice tasks works.
numbers: Three open models, three benchmarks, two memory systems. Mean success: RBC 66.9, whole playbook 55.5, no playbook 54.1, agent's own judgement picks lessons 53.8. A playbook can fall up to 69.6 points below no playbook. Example: 27B ALFWorld first playbook 97.5 vs 74.9 with none; one lesson tagged helpful 123 times, harmful 0 times lowered success. Cutting by the agent's own tags to 40% of tokens left harm in 3 of 4 harmful settings. Budget 40% of tokens; 20% and 60% scored lower.
limits: Needs practice tasks with scores and many episodes per block. Constants were set on four ACE settings and kept on fifteen others. Open models only.
agent_relevance: Admission by self-assessment fails. Use outcome-based valuation of template groups, include or leave out at random on practice problems, and serve the best of curated, whole or none. A 40% token cap beat 20% and 60%.

source: SRA-Bench (2026) Skill Retrieval Augmentation for Agentic AI
finding: Gap 2. A separate measure of 'is the right item retrieved' and 'does the end task improve'. Single-skill retrieval gets only part of the oracle gain, and retrieval accuracy varies widely by task type.
numbers: 5,400 test instances, 636 gold skills hidden among 26,262, six datasets, six models. BM25 Recall@1 / Recall@10: TheoremQA 57.2/80.7; LogicBench 12.0/36.1; ToolQA 7.0/55.1; CHAMP 13.2/36.1; MedCalc 29.3/69.2; BigCodeBench 23.6/61.1. Average accuracy (direct / oracle skill / top-1 full injection / LLM selection): Llama-3.3-70B 47.8 / 64.4 / 52.7 / 59.2; Llama-3.1-8B 29.8 / 44.5 / 32.7 / 37.0; Qwen3-4B 38.8 / 61.6 / 45.5 / 53.3.
limits: Top-3 hit rate is not reported (only R@1 and R@10). Skills are curated how-to documents, not chess-style patterns. The authors say gain depends on retrieval precision at top ranks but is not monotone in retrieval quality.
agent_relevance: With perfect cueing the gain is large (Llama-70B +16.6 pp). Practical retrieval captures roughly 20% to 70% of that gain (top-1 injection about 20-30%, LLM selection about 50-70%). Retrieval accuracy and end gain are separable: log both.

source: SRA-Bench (2026), loading behaviour and top-k
finding: Gap 2 and 6. Models often load a retrieved skill whether or not the right one is there. Adding more full skills (top-k) first helps then hurts.
numbers: Skill loading rate (all 5,400 instances): Qwen3-4B 21.0%, Llama-8B 72.1%, Mistral-24B 28.3%, Qwen3-32B 20.1%, Llama-70B 11.1%, Qwen3-235B 54.1%, GLM-5.1 37.8%, GPT-5.4 31.2%. Load rate when gold skill is in BM25 top-50 vs not: GPT-5.4 36.6% vs 3.6% (+33.0 pp); GLM-5.1 43.5% vs 8.2%; Qwen3-235B 57.8% vs 35.3%; Llama-8B 73.7% vs 64.1%; Llama-70B 10.4% vs 14.5% (-4.2 pp). Full-skill injection improves only at small k then falls (inter-skill interference); progressive disclosure (names first) stays stable.
limits: Figures for the k sweep are plots, not exact numbers in text. Only some models are relevance-aware. The mapping of the overall column to model names follows the table order and was not cross-checked against the prose.
agent_relevance: The pattern-to-candidate step is weak in most open models: loading is poorly tied to whether a good match exists. An explicit retrieve-and-verify step is needed, and a top-k beyond a few full items risks interference.

source: Skill Following (2026) Retrieval-Invoked Actual-Use Effect (RAE)
finding: Gap 2. Separates gain from retrieval from gain from using the content. Many models show positive aggregate lift but negative same-task effect, so the apparent benefit can come from which tasks trigger retrieval.
numbers: 17 LLMs, coding and math. Math500: Llama-3.3-70B +14.2 pp aggregate lift but -39.4 pp RAE; Gemini-2.5-Flash-lite +13.2 vs -11.0. MBPP+: multiple models positive lift, negative RAE. HumanEval+: 3 of 13 models show sign disagreement. Content control on two models: RAE stayed negative with normal, random, corrupted and filler returned content.
limits: RAE conditions only on tasks where the agent chose to retrieve, and the content-control sweep bounds the cause rather than isolating it. Skills here are tool returns, not stored chess-like patterns.
agent_relevance: Report same-task paired effects, not retrieved-vs-skipped averages. The paired arm 'same problem, memory on vs off, only where memory was used' is what separates cueing from extra thinking.

source: ReasoningBank (2025) Scaling Agent Self-Evolving with Reasoning Memory, number of retrieved experiences
finding: Gap 6. One retrieved strategy item gave the best result. Adding more lowered success. The authors conclude relevance and quality matter more than quantity.
numbers: WebArena-Shopping, Gemini-2.5-flash success rate vs number of retrieved experiences: 0 items 39.0; 1 item 49.7; 2 items 46.5; 3 items 45.5; 4 items 44.4. Token cost: about +4.3% total tokens for +20.5% performance vs no memory (appendix C.2).
limits: One subset, one model. Items are short strategy notes, not rich templates, and tokens grow with k, so this is not an equal-token test of '3 rich vs 8 small'. No sweep above 4.
agent_relevance: Evidence against 'more small items'. Does not test the template-theory claim that a few big items beat many small ones at equal tokens; that arm is still to be built.

source: ReasoningBank (2025), Mind2Web cross-task / cross-website / cross-domain
finding: Gap 3. Abstract strategy memory kept its gain across three distance levels, while concrete workflow memory (AWM) lost it at the farthest level.
numbers: Gemini-2.5-flash, step-success rate: no memory 40.3 / 31.7 / 31.9; ReasoningBank 44.9 / 33.9 / 36.6 (cross-task / cross-website / cross-domain; gains +4.6 / +2.2 / +4.7). Element accuracy: 46.0 -> 52.1 / 39.8 -> 44.3 / 35.8 -> 40.6. AWM element accuracy 46.3 / 39.1 / 33.3 (below no-memory at website and domain levels). Task success rates are tiny (1.0 to 4.8%). WebArena Multi subset (cross-site): +4.6 over strongest baseline; AWM no gain.
limits: Distance is a coarse three-level label, not a measured similarity. Full-task success is near the floor, so step metrics carry the result. One model family in the quoted block.
agent_relevance: No steep fall with distance for abstract strategies, but gains are small (2 to 5 points). Still no real far-domain test (e.g. chess to maths).

source: Wang et al. (2024) Agent Workflow Memory (AWM)
finding: Gaps 1 and 3. The only direct comparison found between an abstracted (variables replaced) workflow and a concrete one, and distance results for the same method.
numbers: Workflow induction replaces example values ('dry cat food' -> {product-name}). WebArena (gpt-4): rule-based concrete 35.6 vs LM-abstracted 35.5 total success (steps 6.3 vs 5.9). Mind2Web cross-task: element accuracy 49.5 (rule) vs 50.6 (LM), +2.8 step SR for LM. AWM vs Synapse (retrieved full examples): +5.0 element accuracy, +4.0 step SR. Distance (gpt-4, step SR): MindAct 36.2 / 30.1 / 18.6 vs AWM-offline 45.1 / 33.7 / 32.6 vs AWM-online 43.6 / 33.9 / 35.5 for cross-task / website / domain. Offline-vs-online gap widens with domain gap.
limits: Not equal-token, and the abstracted vs concrete arms differ in more than variables (sub-routine splitting too). Mind2Web success rates are low (0.7 to 4.8%). Offline training workflows degrade when train and test distributions differ.
agent_relevance: Weak support for slots: roughly equal on WebArena, +1 to +3 points on Mind2Web, with confounds. A reusable core with named variables did not fail, but gain over concrete is small. Do not claim a slot advantage yet.

source: Tang et al. (2026) From Memory to Skills: Evidence-Grounded Co-Evolution Governance (MSCE)
finding: Gap 3 and 4. Memory and skills evolved on a source domain helped on a different target domain in every pair tested. Skills are promoted only when evidence-backed and positive-gain.
numbers: EvoAgentBench, five domains (IR, Math, SE, Code, knowledge work). Six transfer pairs: +2.56 to +5.13 Pass@1 points, mean +3.93; cost fell in four of six pairs; transfers into Code cost +4.6% and +8.1% more. Promotion rule: policy needs supporting evidence, positive estimated gain, and consistency with its trigger and boundary. Main results: +15.39 on SE over strongest baseline.
limits: Pairs are among five agent domains, not true far transfer. Which pairs, and per-pair numbers, only in a figure. Evaluation mixes further evolution on the target after initialising from source.
agent_relevance: Cross-domain gain of about 4 points on average is small but positive. Distance dependence not reported, so the gap curve stays unmeasured.

source: Ruoss et al. (2024) Amortized Planning with Large-Scale Transformers: A Case Study on Chess
finding: Gap 9, machine analogue of a search-off arm. Recognition-only networks play at expert-plus level; adding search raises the same network by about 570 to 690 Elo.
numbers: Tournament Elo: Leela Chess Zero policy net only 2292 vs 400 MCTS simulations 2858 (+566); AlphaZero policy only 1777 vs 400 MCTS 2470 (+693); value-net-only Leela 2418, AlphaZero 1992. 270M transformer, no search: tournament Elo 2299 (the Lichess blitz Elo 2895 was vs humans; 2299 vs bots). Puzzle accuracy: transformer 95.4%, Leela policy only 88.6%, with search 99.6%. Under 1.41% of puzzle boards appear in training data.
limits: Tournament Elo is not comparable with Lichess Elo. Puzzles are tactical. Training signal is Stockfish labels, which embed search done offline.
agent_relevance: Pattern knowledge alone gets most of the way; search adds a further large step. The search-off arm in our scaffold is the same idea: first candidate from retrieval alone vs with checked lookahead. It does not settle the human debate.

source: Gobet (2003) Forward search, pattern recognition and visualization in expert chess: reply to Chabris and Hearst (2003)
finding: Gap 7 and 9. Reports the Chabris and Hearst data and Gobet's rebuttal, and gives the only quantitative output of the SEARCH model of pattern-driven move generation.
numbers: Chabris and Hearst: blunders per 1,000 moves (error > 1.5 pawns versus engine) 5.02 classical (about 3 min/move), 6.85 rapid (under 30 s), 7.63 blindfold; classical vs rapid and blindfold significant, rapid vs blindfold not. Gobet: 6x less time gives +36.5% blunders (5.02 -> 6.85), or +0.183% of moves; Kasparov simultaneous median 2682 Elo (IQR 203.5, includes four extra matches). SEARCH (Gobet 1997) with 150,000 chunks (about grandmaster level): moves generated 15% by heuristics, 23% by chunks, 62% by templates.
limits: The SEARCH percentages are a model output, not behavioural data. This is a reply paper; the original Chabris and Hearst PDF was not retrievable this session (404). Possible player and game dependence in blunders. No numbers for CHUMP itself were found.
agent_relevance: Blunders rise only about a third under 6x less time, which fits strong recognition plus modest search. For gap 7: the candidate-move table idea exists in the model (62% from templates) but no held-out hit rate is published in what we could open.

source: Linhares & Brum (2007) Understanding our understanding of strategic scenarios: what role do chunks play? Cognitive Science 31(6), 989-1007
finding: Gap 10. Only the abstract was available (Crossref record; the publisher page returned 403, no open copy). It argues chess players see strong similarity between very different positions when pieces keep the same abstract roles.
numbers: No numbers could be read (abstract only).
quote: chess players are able to perceive strong similarity between very different positions if the pieces retain the same abstract roles
limits: Abstract only. Sample sizes, conditions and effect sizes unknown. The result is against a pieces-on-squares view of chunks, yet Saariluoma-style hybrid results (see K07) leave both views alive.
agent_relevance: Role-based abstraction as a retrieval key is plausible, and AWM and ReasoningBank (d16, d17) give indirect support for it. No surface-change test with an LLM has been found.

source: Yang et al. (2024) Buffer of Thoughts: Thought-Augmented Reasoning with LLMs (retrieval design and ablation)
finding: Gap 2. BoT retrieves exactly one template by embedding similarity with a threshold, then instantiates it. Ablations remove the meta-buffer, the problem distiller and the buffer manager, but they do not score whether the retrieved template was the right one.
numbers: Retrieval: j = argmax similarity between the distilled problem and each template description, accepted only if similarity is at least a threshold (0.5 to 0.7 recommended); below it the task counts as new. Buffer-manager ablation: four rounds of 50 questions per benchmark; with the manager accuracy rises each round, without it no upward trend. The meta-buffer and problem-distiller ablations are plots (values not reliably read from the PDF text).
limits: No top-3 hit rate, no oracle-template arm, no split of gain into 'right template' and 'extra reasoning from the template'. Chart values not extracted.
agent_relevance: The structure is already one retrieved core instantiated with task variables, so it is the nearest existing slot-filled design, but its retrieval accuracy is untested. Build the hit-rate measure before trusting it.
